questions.stem: In the best-known Roman foundation legend, the city was founded by:
options: Romulus, who killed his twin brother Remus
Aeneas, who landed at Ostia after the fall of Carthage
Numa Pompilius, who was chosen by the Sabines
Lucius Junius Brutus, after the expulsion of the kings
questions.explanation: In the legend the twins, sons of Mars and the Vestal Rhea Silvia, were suckled by a she-wolf; Romulus founded the city, traditionally in 753 BCE, and killed Remus. Aeneas was the Trojan ancestor of the Romans in a separate legend, and Numa was the second king.

questions.stem: In his preface, Livy says the traditions about Rome before its founding suit poetic tales better than reliable records, and he will neither confirm nor refute them. For a historian, this means Livy's account of early Rome:
options: is reliable because Livy copied the official records kept by the first kings
should be ignored, since Livy invented all of it himself
was written by an eyewitness who lived in the time of the kings
preserves what Romans believed about their origins, not tested fact
questions.explanation: Livy wrote under Augustus, centuries after the events, and openly admits that the earliest stories are legend. They are valuable for Roman values and identity, and they must be weighed against archaeology for what actually happened.

questions.stem: Livy says that most written records of early Rome were destroyed when the Gauls burned the city. This matters for historians because:
options: later writers had few documents for the period before the sack
it proves that no Romans could read or write before the sack
the Gauls carried off the records and kept them in Gaul
it means archaeology can tell us nothing about early Rome
questions.explanation: If most records were lost, Livy and other later writers depended heavily on family traditions and earlier annalists, which weakens their reliability for the regal and early republican periods. Archaeology and early inscriptions become especially important.

questions.stem: The paterfamilias in Roman society was:
options: the eldest son, who governed the household once he reached adulthood
the oldest living male of a family, with legal power over its members
a priest who conducted the family's sacrifices to the household gods
a magistrate who registered families and their property in the census
questions.explanation: The paterfamilias held patria potestas over his children, his sons' children and his slaves, including, in law, power of life and death. A son remained under it, even as an adult, until his father died unless he was formally released.

questions.stem: In a Roman marriage sine manu (without manus), the wife:
options: could not inherit anything from her own father's family
was given full voting rights in the Roman assemblies
remained under her father's legal authority, not her husband's
became the legal property of her husband, along with all of her dowry
questions.explanation: In a marriage with manus the wife passed into her husband's authority, but in a marriage sine manu, the more common form by the later Republic, she stayed in her father's potestas. In neither case could women vote.

questions.stem: Livy tells how Lucretia, a Roman noblewoman, killed herself after being raped by the king's son, leading to the fall of the monarchy. Livy presents her mainly as:
options: a model of female virtue, whose story gave the revolution a moral cause
a priestess of Vesta who had broken her vows and so was punished
a queen who ruled Rome in her own name before the kings were expelled
a warning to Roman women against interfering in the affairs of state
questions.explanation: For Livy, Lucretia embodied pudicitia (chastity) and her death showed the tyranny of the Tarquins, prompting Brutus to lead the uprising. Such stories were exempla, models of behaviour for Roman readers.

questions.stem: The Vestal Virgins were:
options: slave women who served in the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
the daughters of the early kings, who acted as their chief religious advisers
priestesses who kept the sacred fire of Vesta burning for the city
the wives of the consuls, who led sacrifices on the Capitol
questions.explanation: Six Vestals tended the sacred hearth of the state, which was linked to Rome's survival. They were freed from patria potestas, but a Vestal found to have broken her vow of chastity was buried alive.

questions.stem: The main aim of Roman state religion was to maintain:
options: each citizen's personal hope of a reward from the gods in a life after death
the authority of the kings as living gods ruling over Rome
the supremacy of one god over all the other gods of Italy
the pax deorum, the right relationship between Rome and its gods
questions.explanation: Roman religion was a public duty: correct ritual, sacrifice and the taking of auspices kept the gods' goodwill, which was believed to secure Rome's success. Disasters were often read as signs that the pax deorum had been broken.

questions.stem: In the relationship between patrons and clients, a client usually:
options: paid his patron a fixed yearly rent in exchange for a small farm to work on
was a slave owned by the patron and bound to work in his household
was a foreign king allied to Rome who sent tribute to the senate
gave his patron political support in return for legal and financial help
questions.explanation: Clients greeted their patron each morning (the salutatio), escorted him in public and voted for him, while the patron protected their interests in law and helped them in need. The bond was hereditary and important in Roman politics.

questions.stem: The Twelve Tables declared that a patron who defrauded his client was to be ‘accursed’ (sacer). This law suggests that the patron–client relationship:
options: gave clients the right to vote in the senate on their patron's behalf
carried religious as well as social obligations that bound the patron
was a purely commercial contract that could be ended by either side
was imposed on the patricians by the plebeian tribunes after 287 BCE
questions.explanation: Making a fraudulent patron sacer placed him outside the gods' protection, so the bond was sacred, not just a matter of convenience. The Twelve Tables date from 451–450 BCE, long before 287, and clients had no place in the senate.

questions.stem: A Roman slave who was formally freed (manumitted) by a citizen owner:
options: returned to his homeland and lost all connection with his owner
became a full patrician eligible to stand for election as consul
remained a slave in law but was allowed to marry and own land
became a freedman with citizenship and duties to his former master
questions.explanation: Freed slaves of citizens became citizens themselves, though with limits, and their former master became their patron, to whom they owed respect and services. Slavery at Rome was harsh, but manumission was common, especially for household slaves.

questions.stem: Polybius describes noble funerals at which actors wore the masks of the dead man's ancestors and their deeds were recited. He believed this custom:
options: was meant to frighten the plebeians into obeying the nobles
inspired young Romans to win glory by serving the state
was a Greek practice that the Romans had only just adopted
showed that the Romans worshipped their ancestors as gods
questions.explanation: Polybius, a Greek who lived in Rome, saw these displays of ancestral achievement as a powerful spur to courage and public service. The custom reflects the militarism and competition for glory at the heart of the Roman elite.

questions.stem: According to tradition, Rome's last king, expelled in 509 BCE, was:
options: Lucius Tarquinius Priscus
Tarquinius Superbus
Servius Tullius
Numa Pompilius
questions.explanation: Tarquinius Superbus (‘the Proud’), of Etruscan origin, was remembered as a tyrant, and his son's crime against Lucretia sparked the revolution. Servius Tullius, the sixth king, was credited with the census and the property classes, and Tarquinius Priscus was the fifth.

questions.stem: After the Revolution of 509 BCE, which features of the new Republic were designed to prevent a return to monarchy?
options: a council of plebeian tribunes that chose the king's successor
two consuls elected for one year, each able to block the other
a single consul chosen for life by the senate from the patricians
a king elected every five years by all the citizens in assembly
questions.explanation: Annual office (annuality) and paired magistrates with equal power (collegiality) stopped any one man ruling indefinitely. The king's religious role passed to a priest, the rex sacrorum, who had no political power.

questions.stem: The Lapis Niger, a stone found in the Roman Forum, carries an archaic Latin inscription from the sixth century BCE that appears to mention a ‘king’. Its value for historians is that it:
options: records the text of the Twelve Tables in its original wording
gives early independent evidence that Rome was once ruled by kings
proves that each of Livy's seven kings ruled for the years he gives
shows that Rome was founded by Greek settlers from southern Italy
questions.explanation: The inscription supports the literary tradition that Rome had kings, but it is fragmentary and cannot confirm individual reigns or Livy's details. Corroborating the tradition in general while leaving specifics uncertain is typical of the evidence for early Rome.

questions.stem: The Conflict of the Orders, from 494 to 287 BCE, was a struggle in which:
options: Rome's Latin and Italian allies fought for Roman citizenship and the vote
patricians tried to restore the monarchy of the Tarquins
plebeians sought legal protection and access to political office
the senate fought the consuls for control of the Roman army
questions.explanation: Plebeians pressed the patricians for protection from abuse, published laws, relief from debt and the right to hold magistracies and priesthoods. The allies' struggle for citizenship was the later Social War.

questions.stem: The First Secession of the Plebs in 494 BCE led to the creation of:
options: the tribunes of the plebs, whose persons were sacrosanct
the office of dictator, chosen by the plebeians in a crisis
the Twelve Tables, written by a board of plebeian magistrates
the comitia centuriata, in which every citizen had an equal vote
questions.explanation: By withdrawing from the city, the plebeians forced recognition of their own officials, the tribunes, who could protect plebeians from magistrates and were sacrosanct. The Twelve Tables came about 40 years later, drawn up by the decemvirs.

questions.stem: The Twelve Tables of 451–450 BCE were significant mainly because they:
options: abolished the senate and gave its powers to the tribal assembly
put Rome's laws in writing and on public display for all citizens
gave plebeians the right to be elected as one of the two consuls
made the decisions of the plebeian assembly binding on all citizens
questions.explanation: Publishing the law limited patrician magistrates' freedom to interpret unwritten custom in their own favour. The plebeian consulship came in 367 BCE and binding plebiscites in 287 BCE.

questions.stem: The Licinian–Sextian laws of 367 BCE were a major plebeian gain because they:
options: created the tribunes of the plebs
published the laws of the Twelve Tables
abolished slavery for debt in Rome
opened the consulship to plebeians
questions.explanation: The laws allowed one consul to be plebeian, and Lucius Sextius became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE. The tribunes dated from 494 BCE, and debt bondage was abolished separately in the late fourth century.

questions.stem: The Lex Hortensia of 287 BCE is seen as the end of the Conflict of the Orders because it:
options: allowed patricians and plebeians to marry each other legally
gave the tribunes of the plebs the right to command the armies
made resolutions of the plebeian assembly binding on all citizens
admitted plebeians to the senate for the very first time in Rome
questions.explanation: Once plebiscites bound patricians too, the plebeian assembly became a full law-making body. Intermarriage had been allowed by the Lex Canuleia of 445 BCE, and plebeians had sat in the senate well before 287.

questions.stem: Some historians argue that the Conflict of the Orders did not make Rome a democracy. Which outcome best supports this view?
options: wealthy plebeians joined patricians in a new ruling nobility
the tribunes were abolished once plebeians became consuls
patricians kept sole control of every magistracy until 133
the plebeian assembly was dissolved after the Lex Hortensia
questions.explanation: The main winners were rich plebeian families who, once they held the consulship, merged with the patricians in a nobility (nobiles) that dominated office. The tribunate and the plebeian assembly survived, and plebeians held the consulship from 366.

questions.stem: In the Roman Republic, the senate:
options: was elected each year by all citizens voting in the tribal assembly
passed every law of the Republic, while the assemblies could only advise it
was made up only of the tribunes of the plebs and the two consuls
advised magistrates and in practice controlled finance and foreign policy
questions.explanation: The senate, composed largely of former magistrates, issued advice (senatus consulta) that carried great authority (auctoritas), and it managed the treasury, provinces and relations with foreign states. Laws were passed by the assemblies, not the senate.

questions.stem: The comitia centuriata elected consuls and praetors and voted on war. It favoured the wealthy because:
options: only patricians were allowed to attend and vote in its meetings
each citizen's vote was weighted by the size of his household
its decisions had to be approved by the tribunes before they took effect
its voting units were organised by wealth, and the richest voted first
questions.explanation: Citizens voted in centuries based on property, and the cavalry and first class together held a majority of the 193 centuries, so the poorer centuries often never voted. Plebeians as well as patricians belonged to it.

questions.stem: The usual order of the main offices of the cursus honorum, from lowest to highest, was:
options: praetor, quaestor, consul, aedile
aedile, consul, quaestor, praetor
consul, praetor, aedile, quaestor
quaestor, aedile, praetor, consul
questions.explanation: A Roman politician typically began as quaestor, could serve as aedile, then rose to praetor and finally consul. The Lex Villia Annalis of 180 BCE set minimum ages for these offices.

questions.stem: Polybius explained Rome's success partly through its constitution. He described it as:
options: a monarchy disguised behind elected annual magistrates
a mixed constitution balancing consuls, senate and people
a pure democracy in which the people decided every issue
an oligarchy in which the senate held all power alone
questions.explanation: Polybius saw monarchic (the consuls), aristocratic (the senate) and democratic (the assemblies) elements checking one another, which he believed made Rome stable. Each of the other options takes one element as the whole.

questions.stem: Rome's site helped it grow from a group of villages into a city because it:
options: lay at a crossing of the Tiber, on routes between Etruria and Latium
was the only harbour on the western coast of Italy deep enough for ships
sat on rich silver mines that paid for its early armies and temples
was surrounded by marshes that kept out every invader until the Gauls
questions.explanation: The hills by the Tiber crossing, near the river's mouth and the salt beds, gave Rome a position on trade routes between the Etruscans and the Latins. The marshy valley of the Forum was drained and paved as the settlement became a city.

questions.stem: Land captured in Rome's wars often became ager publicus (public land). This caused tension because:
options: it was used solely for temples, so it reduced the land for farming
it was sold to Carthage to pay the costs of the wars against Pyrrhus
much of it was occupied by the wealthy, while poorer citizens wanted shares
it was given only to foreign allies and never to any Roman citizens at all
questions.explanation: Public land was meant to belong to the Roman people, but wealthy families occupied and farmed large tracts of it, while small farmers and plebeians demanded land. The issue ran from the early Republic to the Gracchi.

questions.stem: Under nexum, an early Roman form of debt contract:
options: the state paid the debts of any citizen who served in the legions
debts were cancelled automatically every seven years by the censors
creditors were forbidden to charge interest on loans to plebeians
a debtor who could not repay could be held in bondage by his creditor
questions.explanation: Debt bondage was a major plebeian grievance in the Conflict of the Orders, and it was abolished in the late fourth century BCE. The other arrangements did not exist in Rome.

questions.stem: After the Second Punic War and the eastern wars, huge numbers of captives were brought to Italy as slaves. The main economic consequence was:
options: the growth of large estates worked by slaves, at the expense of small farmers
the end of farming in Italy, since all grain was now imported from Carthage
a fall in the wealth of the senatorial class as slaves replaced free labour
the abolition of the census, since slaves could not be counted as property
questions.explanation: Wealthy Romans invested war profits in land and worked it with cheap slave labour, while small farmers, away on long campaigns, struggled to compete. This widened the gap between rich and poor that later fed the crisis of the Republic.

questions.stem: The Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, was:
options: a wall built around the city after the Gallic sack
a canal joining the Tiber to the port of Ostia
a road linking Rome to Capua, used to move armies and goods
an aqueduct bringing fresh water to Rome from the springs of the Alban Hills
questions.explanation: The road, built during the Second Samnite War, let Roman armies reach Campania quickly and bound the region to Rome. Appius Claudius also built Rome's first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, which is a different project.

questions.stem: After the Battle of Lake Regillus, Rome made a treaty with the Latins, the Foedus Cassianum of 493 BCE. Its main terms were:
options: Latin submission to Rome and the payment of a yearly tribute in silver
full Roman citizenship for every Latin who served in the legions
the transfer of all Latin land to Rome as public land for its farmers
mutual defence and a shared division of the booty from joint wars
questions.explanation: The treaty created a defensive alliance of equals in which Rome and the Latins fought together and shared the spoils. It did not impose tribute, and citizenship for the Latins came much later.

questions.stem: The capture of the Etruscan city of Veii, traditionally in 396 BCE under Camillus, was significant because it:
options: ended the Conflict of the Orders by giving its land to the plebeians
was the first time Rome had defeated a Greek army in Italy
greatly enlarged Rome's territory and showed it could besiege a major city
made Rome a sea power for the first time, with a fleet strong enough to fight Carthage
questions.explanation: Taking Veii roughly doubled Rome's territory, and Livy links the long siege to the introduction of pay for soldiers. Rome's first fleet came in the First Punic War, and its first war against a Greek army was against Pyrrhus.

questions.stem: After defeating the Romans at the Allia, the Gauls sacked Rome, traditionally in about 390 BCE. A long-term result was that the Romans:
options: paid the Gauls tribute every year until the First Punic War
gave up expansion in Italy and concentrated on trade by sea
built a strong stone wall around the city and rebuilt their power
abandoned Rome and moved their capital to the captured city of Veii
questions.explanation: The sack was a deep humiliation, but Rome recovered and built a large stone wall, later called the Servian Wall, in the decades after. Livy reports a proposal to move to Veii, which Camillus is said to have defeated.

questions.stem: In 321 BCE, during the Second Samnite War, a Roman army trapped at the Caudine Forks surrendered and was forced to pass under a yoke. Rome's response was to:
options: invite Pyrrhus of Epirus to help it defeat the Samnites
accept Samnite rule and pay tribute for twenty years
reject the peace, rebuild its army and extend roads and colonies
abandon Campania permanently and leave the whole region to the Samnites
questions.explanation: Rome recovered from the humiliation, building the Via Appia and founding colonies to encircle the Samnites, and won the war in 304 BCE. Pyrrhus came later, invited by Tarentum against Rome.

questions.stem: Pyrrhus of Epirus defeated Rome at Heraclea (280 BCE) and Asculum (279 BCE), yet a ‘Pyrrhic victory’ came to mean a win that costs too much. This is because:
options: Rome bribed his generals to stop fighting after each battle
Carthage seized Epirus while Pyrrhus was fighting in Italy
his heavy losses could not be replaced, while Rome kept raising armies
he was killed at Asculum, and his leaderless army returned home to Epirus
questions.explanation: Plutarch reports Pyrrhus saying another such victory would ruin him: he lost experienced troops he could not replace, whereas Rome drew on the manpower of its citizens and allies. After Beneventum in 275 he withdrew, and Rome controlled southern Italy.

questions.stem: Rome's Italian allies paid no tribute but supplied soldiers for Rome's wars. Why was this system a major source of Roman strength?
options: it gave Rome huge reserves of manpower and a shared stake in victory
it allowed Rome to fight every war without any Roman citizens serving
it made the allies full Roman citizens with the right to vote in Rome
it meant Rome never needed to found colonies or build roads in Italy
questions.explanation: Allied troops, alongside Roman citizens, let Rome replace even catastrophic losses, and allies shared in booty and protection. Most allies did not receive full citizenship until after the Social War of 91–88 BCE.

questions.stem: The First Punic War began in 264 BCE when Rome intervened in:
options: Sicily, after the Mamertines of Messana appealed for help
Spain, after Hannibal attacked the town of Saguntum
North Africa, after Carthage attacked Rome's ally Numidia
Greece, after Carthage made an alliance with Macedon
questions.explanation: The Mamertines, mercenaries holding Messana, appealed to Rome, and Roman intervention brought war with Carthage over Sicily. Saguntum began the Second Punic War and the war with Masinissa of Numidia the Third.

questions.stem: At the end of the First Punic War in 241 BCE, Carthage:
options: gave up Spain and handed Hannibal to Rome
was destroyed and its land made a province
gave up Sicily and paid Rome a large indemnity
lost its fleet and was forbidden to wage war
questions.explanation: After the Roman naval victory at the Aegates Islands, Carthage evacuated Sicily, which became Rome's first overseas province, and paid an indemnity. The other terms belong to the end of the Second and Third Punic Wars.

questions.stem: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal destroyed a large Roman army by:
options: ambushing the Romans in a fog beside the shore of Lake Trasimene
using elephants to break through the Roman lines in the Alps
letting his centre fall back and enveloping the Romans from both sides
luring the Roman fleet into a narrow strait and ramming its ships one by one
questions.explanation: Hannibal's centre gave ground while his African infantry closed on the flanks and his cavalry attacked the rear, trapping the Romans in a double envelopment. The fog ambush was at Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE.

questions.stem: Despite the disasters at Trasimene and Cannae, Rome was not defeated by Hannibal. The most important reason was that:
options: Carthage recalled Hannibal immediately after his victory at Cannae
Philip V of Macedon joined Rome and invaded Carthage from the east
most of Rome's allies in central Italy and the Latin colonies stayed loyal
Hannibal captured Rome itself but could not hold it against the Roman fleet
questions.explanation: Capua and many southern allies defected, but the core of the alliance held, so Rome kept its manpower and Hannibal could not break it without siege equipment or steady reinforcements. Fabius Maximus's delaying strategy helped Rome rebuild, and Hannibal stayed in Italy until 203.

questions.stem: The peace that ended the Second Punic War in 201 BCE weakened Carthage most lastingly because it:
options: made Hannibal a Roman citizen and an ally of the senate
turned all of North Africa into a single Roman province
barred Carthage from waging war without Rome's permission
required Carthage to move its city ten miles from the sea
questions.explanation: Carthage lost Spain, most of its fleet and paid a heavy indemnity, but the ban on war without Roman consent left it exposed to Masinissa of Numidia. The demand to move inland was made in 149 BCE, at the start of the Third Punic War.

questions.stem: The Third Punic War (149–146 BCE) was triggered when:
options: Carthage seized Sicily from Rome while Rome fought in Greece
Carthage refused to pay any more of its indemnity to Rome
Carthage fought Masinissa of Numidia, breaking the treaty of 201
Hannibal returned from exile to lead a new invasion of Italy
questions.explanation: When Carthage took up arms against Masinissa's raids, Rome treated it as a breach of the treaty. Cato the Elder had long urged that Carthage be destroyed, and in 146 BCE Scipio Aemilianus razed the city.

questions.stem: In 146 BCE, the same year Carthage was destroyed, Rome sacked Corinth. The conquest of Greece was significant for Rome because it:
options: made Greek the official language of the Roman senate and courts
led Rome to adopt the Athenian democracy as its own constitution
brought Greek art, learning and wealth, and many slaves, into Rome
ended Roman interest in the eastern Mediterranean for a century
questions.explanation: Greek culture deeply influenced Roman literature, art, religion and education, while plunder and slaves enriched the elite. Some Romans, such as Cato, criticised Greek influence as a threat to traditional Roman values.

questions.stem: Polybius, a Greek taken to Rome as a hostage in 167 BCE, became a friend of Scipio Aemilianus and saw the destruction of Carthage. A historian using his work should weigh:
options: his loyalty to Carthage against his use of Roman documents
his late date, centuries after the Punic Wars he described
his first-hand knowledge against his closeness to the Scipios
his ignorance of Rome against his access to Carthaginian records
questions.explanation: Polybius knew leading Romans, visited sites and witnessed events, which makes him invaluable, but his friendship with the Scipios may colour his judgements of them. He aimed to explain how Rome came to rule almost the whole known world in under 53 years.
